dmm-2020-power-01.title: Solve for y
dmm-2020-power-01.body:
Clearing denominators in $\frac{10x+y}{10y+z}=\frac xz$ gives $10xz+yz=10xy+xz$, i.e. $9xz=y(10x-z)$. Put $d=10x-z\ (>0)$; then $z=10x-d$ and
$$y=\frac{9xz}{d}=\frac{90x^2}{d}-9x.$$
So $d$ must divide $90x^2$, and $1\le z\le9$, $1\le y\le9$ give $10x-9\le d\le 10x-1$ and $d\ge\frac{10x^2}{x+1}$.

* $x=1$: $d\in[5,9]$ with $d\mid90$: $d=5$ gives $(1,9,5)$; $d=6$ gives $(1,6,4)$; $d=9$ gives $(1,1,1)$ (trivial).
* $x=2$: $d\in[14,19]$, $d\mid360$: $d=15$ gives $(2,6,5)$; $d=18$ gives $(2,2,2)$ (trivial).
* $x=3$: $d\in[23,29]$, $d\mid810$: only $d=27$, giving $(3,3,3)$.
* $x=4$: $d\in[32,39]$, $d\mid1440$: $d=32$ gives $(4,9,8)$; $d=36$ gives $(4,4,4)$.
* $x=5,\dots,9$: the only admissible divisor is $d=10x-x=9x$, giving the trivial $(x,x,x)$.

So the lucky triples are $(1,6,4),(1,9,5),(2,6,5),(4,9,8)$. Check: $\frac{19}{95}=\frac15$, $\frac{26}{65}=\frac25$, $\frac{49}{98}=\frac12$.

**Answer: $(1,9,5),(2,6,5),(4,9,8)$**

dmm-2020-power-01.title: Brute force check
dmm-2020-power-01.body:
Testing all $9^3=729$ digit triples with the condition $(10x+y)\,z=x\,(10y+z)$ (equivalently $\frac{xy}{yz}=\frac xz$ as two-digit numbers) gives exactly the four triples $(1,6,4),(1,9,5),(2,6,5),(4,9,8)$, so the other three are $(1,9,5),(2,6,5),(4,9,8)$.

**Answer: $(1,9,5),(2,6,5),(4,9,8)$**

dmm-2020-power-02a.title: Check every triple
dmm-2020-power-02a.body:
The digits $x,y,z\in\{1,2\}$, not all equal, give the six triples $(1,1,2),(1,2,1),(2,1,1),(1,2,2),(2,1,2),(2,2,1)$. The condition is $(3x+y)z=x(3y+z)$. Left and right sides are:

| triple | $(3x+y)z$ | $x(3y+z)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $(1,1,2)$ | 8 | 5 |
| $(1,2,1)$ | 5 | 7 |
| $(2,1,1)$ | 7 | 8 |
| $(1,2,2)$ | 10 | 8 |
| $(2,1,2)$ | 14 | 10 |
| $(2,2,1)$ | 8 | 14 |

No row has equal entries, so $\lambda(3)=0$ (this also follows from Problem 5 since $3$ is prime).

**Answer: 0**

dmm-2020-power-02b.title: Bound the products
dmm-2020-power-02b.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

For $b=4$, (L1) reads $4x(z-y)=z(x-y)$. If $z=y$ then $z(x-y)=0$ forces $x=y$ (trivial), so $z\ne y$ and similarly $x\ne y$. Then $|z(x-y)|=4x|z-y|$ is a positive multiple of $4$. But $z\le3$ and $|x-y|\le2$ give $|z(x-y)|\le6$, so $|z(x-y)|=4$ and $x|z-y|=1$. Hence $x=1$, $|z-y|=1$, and $z|1-y|=4$ with $z\le3$, $|1-y|\le2$ forces $z=2$, $y=3$. Check: $\frac{4\cdot1+3}{4\cdot3+2}=\frac7{14}=\frac12=\frac12$.

The only lucky $4$-triple is $(1,3,2)$, so $\lambda(4)=1$.

**Answer: 1**

dmm-2020-power-02c.title: Case on the value of $z(x-y)$
dmm-2020-power-02c.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

For $b=6$: $6x(z-y)=z(x-y)$ with $x,y,z\le5$. As before $x\ne y$, $z\ne y$, and $|z(x-y)|=6x|z-y|\le5\cdot4=20$ is a positive multiple of $6$: $6$, $12$ or $18$ ($18$ would need $z\cdot|x-y|=18$ with $z\le5$, $|x-y|\le4$, impossible).

* $6$: $x|z-y|=1$ so $x=1$, $|z-y|=1$; and $z|1-y|=6$: $(z,|1-y|)=(2,3)$ or $(3,2)$, giving $y=4$ (then $|z-y|=2$) or $y=3$ (then $|z-y|=0$): both fail.
* $12$: $x|z-y|=2$ and $z|x-y|=12$, so $(z,|x-y|)=(3,4)$ or $(4,3)$. For $z=3$: $x=1,y=5$ gives $|z-y|=2$, $x|z-y|=2$ and the signs agree ($z<y$, $x<y$): $(1,5,3)$ works. For $z=4$: $x=2,y=5$ gives $|z-y|=1$, $x|z-y|=2$, signs agree: $(2,5,4)$ works. The other choices of $(x,y)$ fail.

So the lucky $6$-triples are $(1,5,3)$ and $(2,5,4)$ (check: $\frac{6+5}{30+3}=\frac{11}{33}=\frac13$ and $\frac{12+5}{30+4}=\frac{17}{34}=\frac12=\frac24$). Hence $\lambda(6)=2$.

**Answer: 2**

dmm-2020-power-02d.title: Case on the value of $z(x-y)$
dmm-2020-power-02d.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

For $b=9$: $9x(z-y)=z(x-y)$, $x,y,z\le8$. Again $x\ne y\ne z$. The common absolute value $k=9x|z-y|=z|x-y|$ is a multiple of $9$ and at most $8\cdot7=56$, and the signs of $z-y$ and $x-y$ must agree. We examine $k=9,18,27,36,45,54$ using $z|x-y|=k$, $z\le 8$, $|x-y|\le7$:

* $k=9$: $x|z-y|=1$, $z|x-y|=9$ gives $x=1$, $z=3$, $y=4$ (sign check $z<y$, $x<y$): $(1,4,3)$ works.
* $k=18$: $z\in\{3,6\}$; every candidate fails either $x|z-y|=2$ or the sign condition.
* $k=27,45,54$: $z|x-y|=k$ has no solution with $z\le8,\ |x-y|\le7$.
* $k=36$: $z=6$, $|x-y|=6$, $x|z-y|=4$ gives $(x,y)=(2,8)$ (signs agree: $z<y$, $x<y$): $(2,8,6)$ works.

Check: $\frac{9+4}{36+3}=\frac{13}{39}=\frac13$ and $\frac{18+8}{72+6}=\frac{26}{78}=\frac13=\frac26$. So $\lambda(9)=2$.

**Answer: 2**

dmm-2020-power-02d.title: Direct check
dmm-2020-power-02d.body:
Testing all $8^3=512$ triples directly in $(9x+y)z=x(9y+z)$ gives exactly $(1,4,3)$ and $(2,8,6)$, so $\lambda(9)=2$.

**Answer: 2**

dmm-2020-power-03.title: Check all bases below 10
dmm-2020-power-03.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

We know $\lambda(10)=4$ (Problem 1), and $\lambda(2)=0$ (the only digit is $1$, so only the trivial triple), $\lambda(3)=0$, $\lambda(4)=1$, $\lambda(6)=2$, $\lambda(9)=2$ (Problem 2). For primes $b=5,7$ we have $\lambda(b)=0$ (Problem 5). It remains to find $\lambda(8)$.

For $b=8$, (L2) is $(8x-z)\,y=7xz$. Since $8x-z\equiv x-z\pmod7$ and $x\ne z$ (otherwise (L2) gives $y=x$, trivial), $7\nmid(8x-z)$, so $7\mid y$ and $y=7$. Then $8x-z=xz$, so $z=\frac{8x}{x+1}$ and $x+1\mid8$: $x=1,z=4$; $x=3,z=6$; $x=7,z=7$ (trivial). So $\lambda(8)=2$, with $(1,7,4)$ and $(3,7,6)$.

Thus $\lambda(b)\le2$ for $b\le9$ while $\lambda(10)=4>2$, so the smallest such base is $10$.

**Answer: 10**

dmm-2020-power-04.title: Subtract the two equations
dmm-2020-power-04.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

Suppose $(x,y,z)$ is lucky in bases $b_1\ne b_2$. Then (L1) holds for both:
$$b_1x(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad b_2x(z-y)=z(x-y).$$
Subtracting gives $(b_1-b_2)\,x\,(z-y)=0$. Since $b_1\ne b_2$ and $x\ge1$, we get $z=y$. Then $z(x-y)=0$ with $z\ge1$ gives $x=y$, so $x=y=z$, which is not allowed. Hence no such triple exists. ∎

dmm-2020-power-05.title: Divisibility by p
dmm-2020-power-05.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

Let $p$ be prime and $(x,y,z)$ a lucky $p$-triple. By (L1), $p\mid z(x-y)$. Since $1\le z\le p-1$, $p\nmid z$, so $p\mid x-y$. But $|x-y|\le p-2<p$, hence $x=y$. Then (L1) gives $0=px(z-y)$, so $z=y$ too, and $x=y=z$, which is excluded. So there are no lucky $p$-triples. ∎

dmm-2020-power-06a.title: Use (L2) modulo the prime b-1
dmm-2020-power-06a.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

Let $q=b-1$ be prime. By (L2), $q\mid y(bx-z)$. Since $b\equiv1\pmod q$, $bx-z\equiv x-z\pmod q$, and $|x-z|\le b-2<q$. If $q\mid x-z$ then $x=z$; (L2) then gives $(bx-x)y=(b-1)x^2$, so $y=x$, a trivial triple. Hence $q\nmid(bx-z)$ and so $q\mid y$. As $1\le y\le b-1=q$, we get $y=b-1$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-06b.title: Count the triples with y = b-1
dmm-2020-power-06b.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

By Problem 6(a), every lucky $b$-triple has $y=b-1$. Then (L2) reads $(bx-z)(b-1)=(b-1)xz$, i.e. $bx-z=xz$, which can be rewritten as
$$(x+1)(b-z)=b.$$
So $k=b-z$ is a divisor of $b$ with $k\ge1$; moreover $k=1$ means $z=b-1$ and then $x+1=b$, $x=b-1=y=z$ (trivial), and $k=b$ would mean $z=0$. So $k$ is a proper factor of $b$.

Conversely, each proper factor $k$ of $b$ gives $z=b-k\in[1,b-2]$, $x=\frac bk-1\in[1,b-1)$ and $y=b-1$, satisfying $(x+1)(b-z)=b$; this is not the trivial triple because $x=\frac bk-1<b-1=y$. The maps $k\mapsto(\frac bk-1,\,b-1,\,b-k)$ and the triple $\mapsto b-z$ are inverse to each other, so $\lambda(b)$ equals the number of proper factors of $b$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-06c.title: Exhibit one triple per proper factor
dmm-2020-power-06c.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

For each proper factor $k$ of $b$, let $(x,y,z)=\left(\frac bk-1,\ b-1,\ b-k\right)$. These are integers in $[1,b-1]$, and $x<y$ so the triple is non-trivial. It satisfies (L1): $z-y=1-k$, $x-y=\frac bk-b=\frac{b(1-k)}{k}$, so
$$bx(z-y)=b\left(\frac{b-k}{k}\right)(1-k),\qquad z(x-y)=(b-k)\cdot\frac{b(1-k)}{k},$$
which are equal. Different $k$ give different $z=b-k$, so we get at least as many lucky $b$-triples as proper factors. ∎

dmm-2020-power-06d.title: Halving
dmm-2020-power-06d.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

By Problem 6(c) each proper factor $k$ of $b$ gives the lucky triple $T_k=\left(\frac bk-1,\,b-1,\,b-k\right)$. Since $b$ is odd, $k$ and $\frac bk$ are odd, so all three entries of $T_k$ are even, and since they are positive, halving gives integers $\ge1$. The defining equation (L1) is homogeneous (degree $2$ in $(x,y,z)$), so $\frac12T_k=\left(\frac{b/k-1}2,\frac{b-1}2,\frac{b-k}2\right)$ is again a lucky $b$-triple (it is non-trivial since $x\ne y$).

The triples $\frac12T_k$ have middle entry $\frac{b-1}{2}\ne b-1$, so they differ from every $T_{k'}$. Because $b$ is odd and not prime it has at least one proper factor, so we get at least one more triple than the number of proper factors: $\lambda(b)>\#\{\text{proper factors}\}$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-07a.title: Show z < y, then 2x ≤ z
dmm-2020-power-07a.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

**$z<y$.** If $z=y$, (L1) gives $z(x-y)=0$ so $x=y$, trivial. Suppose $z>y$. Then $bx(z-y)\ge bx>zx>z(x-y)$ because $b>z$ and $y\ge1$, contradicting (L1). So $z<y$ (and then (L1) shows $x<y$).

**$2x\le z$.** Suppose $2x>z$. Then $bx-z>(b-2)x$, so by (L2)
$$(b-1)xz=(bx-z)y>(b-2)xy,\quad\text{so}\quad y<\frac{b-1}{b-2}\,z=z+\frac{z}{b-2}.$$
Since $z<y$ are integers, $y\ge z+1$, hence $\frac{z}{b-2}>1$, i.e. $z>b-2$, so $z=b-1$. But then $y>z=b-1$ is impossible. Therefore $2x\le z<y$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-07b.title: One strict, one sharp
dmm-2020-power-07b.body:
In the proof of 7(a) we showed $z\ne y$ for every lucky triple (otherwise $x=y=z$), so $z<y$ always holds strictly.

The inequality $2x\le z$ cannot be improved to $2x<z$: the lucky $4$-triple $(1,3,2)$ (check: $\frac{4+3}{12+2}=\frac12$) has $2x=2=z$. So only $z<y$ is always strict. ∎

dmm-2020-power-08.title: Use (L2)
dmm-2020-power-08.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

By (L2), $(bx-z)\,y=(b-1)xz$, and $p\mid b-1$, so $p\mid(bx-z)\,y$. As $p$ is prime, $p\mid y$ or $p\mid bx-z$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-09.title: Reduce to a divisibility condition on y
dmm-2020-power-09.body:
Recall that the defining equation $z(bx+y)=x(by+z)$ can be rearranged as
$$\text{(L1)}\quad bx(z-y)=z(x-y),\qquad \text{(L2)}\quad (bx-z)\,y=(b-1)\,xz.$$

Write $l=\frac{b-1}{p}$. Since $bx-z=(b-1)x+(x-z)$ and $p\mid b-1$, $p\mid bx-z$ gives $p\mid x-z$; let $s=\frac{x-z}{p}$. Then $bx-z=p(lx+s)$, and (L2) becomes $p(lx+s)\,y=p\,l\,xz$, so
$$(lx+s)\,y=lxz\quad\Longrightarrow\quad lx\,(z-y)=s\,y.$$
If $s=0$ then $x=z$ and (L2) gives $y=x$, a trivial triple; so $s\ne0$. Since $|x-z|\le b-2<b-1$, we have $|s|<l$. From $lx(z-y)=sy$ we get $l\mid sy$. If $\gcd(l,y)=1$, then $l\mid s$, which with $0<|s|<l$ is impossible. Hence $\gcd(l,y)>1$, and any prime $q\mid\gcd(l,y)$ satisfies $q\mid b-1$ and $q\mid y$. (If $l=1$ the argument shows $|s|<1$, contradicting $s\ne0$, so this case cannot occur.) ∎

dmm-2020-power-10a.title: Solve (L2) for x and z
dmm-2020-power-10a.body:
Substitute $y=pm$ and $b-1=pl$ in (L2) and divide by $p$: $(bx-z)\,m=l\,xz$. Rewrite it as $mz=x(bm-lz)$, so $x\mid mz$ and $k=\frac{mz}{x}$ is an integer, with $mz=xk$. Then $bxm-xk=lxz$, so dividing by $x$,
$$bm-k=lz,\qquad z=\frac{mb-k}{l}.$$
Then $x=\frac{mz}{k}=\frac{m(mb-k)}{kl}=\frac{m^2b-mk}{kl}$, and $y=pm$. Hence
$$(x,y,z)=\left(\frac{m^2b-mk}{kl},\ mp,\ \frac{mb-k}{l}\right).$$
For $(1,6,4)$ in base $10$ with $p=3$, $l=3$: $m=2$, $k=8$, and the formula gives $\left(\frac{40-16}{24},6,\frac{20-8}{3}\right)=(1,6,4)$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-10b.title: Integrality of z
dmm-2020-power-10b.body:
From $z=\frac{mb-k}{l}$ and $b=pl+1$:
$$z=\frac{m(b-1)+m-k}{l}=mp+\frac{m-k}{l}.$$
Since $z$ and $mp$ are integers, $l\mid m-k$, i.e. $k\equiv m\pmod l$. ∎

dmm-2020-power-10c.title: Use x ≥ 1 and z < y
dmm-2020-power-10c.body:
**Upper bound.** Since $x\ge1$, $\frac{m^2b-mk}{kl}\ge1$, so $m^2b\ge k(m+l)$, i.e. $k\le\frac{m^2b}{m+l}$.

**Lower bound.** By Problem 7(a), $z<y=mp$, so $\frac{mb-k}{l}<mp$, i.e. $mb-k<mpl=m(b-1)$, so $k>m$. As $k\equiv m\pmod l$, the smallest possible value is $k=m+l$. (The value $k=m$ would give the trivial triple $x=y=z=mp$.)

So $m+l\le k\le\frac{m^2b}{m+l}$. For the lucky $10$-triple $(1,6,4)$ ($p=3$, $l=3$, $m=2$, $k=8$): $5\le8\le\frac{40}{5}=8$, so both bounds can be attained or nearly so. ∎
